s: Eumolpus is a son of Poseidon
q: This Eumolpus they say came from Thrace, and was the son of Poseidon and Chione

s: Eumolpus is a son of Chione
q: This Eumolpus they say came from Thrace, and was the son of Poseidon and Chione

s: Rheti is sacred to Proserpine
q: These Rheti are said to be sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, and their priests only may catch the fish in them.

s: battle between Eleusis and Athens resulted in death of Erechtheus (king of Athens)
q: And in the battle between the people of Eleusis and the Athenians Erechtheus the king of Athens was slain

s: battle between Eleusis and Athens resulted in death of Immaradus (son of Eumolpus)
q: and also Immaradus the son of Eumolpus

s: Eleusis is a city
q: And the hero Eleusis, from whom the city gets its name, was according to some the son of Hermes and Daira the daughter of Oceanus, others make him the son of Ogygus.

s: Eleusis is named after Eleusis (hero)
q: And the hero Eleusis, from whom the city gets its name, was according to some the son of Hermes and Daira the daughter of Oceanus, others make him the son of Ogygus.

s: Eleusinian mysteries are managed by Eleusinians (privately)
q: and peace was concluded on these conditions, that the people of Eleusis should be in all other respects Athenians, but should have the private management of their Mysteries.

s: Eleusinian mysteries are performed by daughters of Celeus (rites of Demeter and Proserpine)
q: And the rites of the two goddesses, Demeter and Proserpine, were performed by the daughters of Celeus.

s: Theseus killed Polypemon (at Erineus; Polypemon was surnamed Procrustes)
q: On the banks of this river Theseus slew the robber Polypemon, who was surnamed Procrustes.

s: Bœotia has boundary with Attica (at the Platæan district, formerly; later at Mount Cithæron)
q: And as you turn from Eleusis to Bœotia the boundary of Attica is the Platæan district.

s: Eleutheræ became part of Athenians (voluntarily, from hatred of the Thebans and liking for Athenian government)
q: And the people of Eleutheræ became Athenians not by compulsion, but from hatred to the Thebans and a liking for the Athenian form of government.

s: Rheti is sacred to Demeter
q: These Rheti are said to be sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, and their priests only may catch the fish in them.

s: Dionysus has temple at Eleutheræ (the statue there is an imitation of the one removed to Athens)
q: In this plain too is a temple of Dionysus, and a statue of the god was removed thence to Athens long ago: the one at Eleutheræ now is an imitation of it.

s: Megara originally belonged to Athenians (having been bequeathed to Pandion by its king Pylas)
q: Next to Eleusis is the district called Megaris: it too belonged originally to the Athenians, having been bequeathed to Pandion by (its) king Pylas.

s: Megara was taken from Athenians (when Codrus was king)
q: And afterwards, when Codrus was king, the Peloponnesians marched against Athens: and not having any brilliant success there they went home again, but took Megara from the Athenians

s: Megara became dorian Dorians (after its capture and resettlement)
q: Thus the Megarians changed their customs and dialect and became Dorians.

s: Megara is named after Megareus (according to the Boeotian tradition)
q: and the city which had been formerly called Nisa, got its name Megara from him.

s: Thebes was ruled by Creon (as regent for Laodamas)
q: For Creon, who was at that time the ruler at Thebes (being Regent for Laodamas the son of Eteocles)

s: Creon forbade burial of Argives (their relations)
q: would not allow their relations to bury the dead

s: burial of the Theban dead at Eleusis was performed by Theseus (after his victory over the Boeotians)
q: and Adrastus having supplicated Theseus, and a battle having been fought between the Athenians and Bœotians, when Theseus was the victor, he conveyed the dead bodies to Eleusis and there buried them.

s: Alcathous came from Elis (after the death of Nisus and a revolution at Megara)
q: But it is certain that it was not till after the death of Nisus, and a revolution at Megara, that Alcathous came there from Elis.

s: Rheti formed boundary between Eleusinians (in old times)
q: And they were, as I hear, in old times the boundaries between the territory of the Eleusinians and Athenians.

s: Alcathous killed Cithæron lion (and thereby won the kingdom of Megara)
q: So Alcathous (the son of Pelops) attacked the beast and slew him, and, when he became king built this temple

s: Hippolyta was buried Megara
q: and there, having been unsuccessful with her army, and dejected at the present state of things, and still more despondent about getting safe home again to Themiscyra, died of grief and was buried.

s: Amazons were defeated by Theseus (during their expedition against Athens)
q: When the Amazons, on account of Antiope, made an expedition against the Athenians, they were beaten by Theseus

s: Tereus committed suicide at Megara (after his subjects ceased obeying him)
q: And he committed suicide at Megara, and they forthwith piled up a tomb for him

s: Rheti formed boundary between Athenians (in old times)
q: And they were, as I hear, in old times the boundaries between the territory of the Eleusinians and Athenians.

s: Proserpine is sacred to Rheti
q: These Rheti are said to be sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, and their priests only may catch the fish in them.

s: Demeter is sacred to Rheti
q: These Rheti are said to be sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, and their priests only may catch the fish in them.

s: Eleusinians have private management of Eleusinian mysteries (under the peace settlement)
q: and peace was concluded on these conditions, that the people of Eleusis should be in all other respects Athenians, but should have the private management of their Mysteries.

s: Athenians include Eleusinians (in all respects except private management of the Mysteries)
q: and peace was concluded on these conditions, that the people of Eleusis should be in all other respects Athenians, but should have the private management of their Mysteries.

s: Megara has citadel named after Alcathous
q: There is also another citadel at Megara that gets its name from Alcathous.

s: Peribœa accompanied Theseus (to Crete in connection with the tribute)
q: Peribœa the daughter of Alcathous was certainly sent by him to Crete with Theseus in connection with the tribute.

s: Megara was numbered among Athenians (according to the stated evidence)
q: And the following fact proves that the Megarians were numbered among the Athenians:

s: Megareus has monument at Megara
q: As one goes up to it, there is on the right hand a monument of Megareus, who started from Onchestus to aid the Megarians in the Cretan War.

s: Timalcus was killed by Theseus
q: the tomb of Timalcus, who, as I said a little time back, was killed by Theseus.

s: Athene has temple at Megara (on the hill where the citadel stands)
q: And on the hill where the citadel stands is a temple of Athene, and a brazen statue of the goddess, except the hands and the toes, which as well as the face are of ivory.

s: Athene has statue material ivory (face, hands, and toes)
q: a brazen statue of the goddess, except the hands and the toes, which as well as the face are of ivory.

s: Emperor Adrian built old temple of Apollo (of white stone)
q: but afterwards the Emperor Adrian built it of white stone.

s: Callipolis was killed by Alcathous (after throwing wood from Apollo’s altar)
q: And Alcathous, not having yet heard the news about Ischepolis, was vexed with Callipolis for his irreverence, and in his wrath killed him instantaneously by striking him on the head with one of the pieces of wood he had thrown down from the altar.

s: Ino has hero chapel at Megara (on the road to the Prytaneum)
q: On the road to the Prytaneum there is a hero-chapel of Ino, and a cornice of stone round it.

s: Iphigenia has mortuary chapel at Megara (according to the Megarians)
q: They also lay claim to the possession of a mortuary-chapel of Iphigenia, for she too they say died at Megara.

s: Iphigenia was changed into Hecate (according to Hesiod’s Catalogue of Women, by Artemis’s will)
q: Hesiod in his Catalogue of Women describes Iphigenia as not dying, but being changed into Hecate by the will of Artemis.

s: Adrastus has divine honours at Megara
q: Adrastus also has divine honours among the Megarians:

s: Adrastus died at Megara (of old age and sorrow for Ægialeus)
q: he too they say died among them (when he was leading the army back after the capture of Thebes), of old age and sorrow for the death of Ægialeus.

s: Æsymnus consulted Delphi (about how the Megarians might prosper)
q: Then it was that Æsymnus, second to none of the Megarians in fame and influence, went to Apollo at Delphi, and asked how they were to have prosperity.

s: Megara replaced kingship with chief magistrates annually chosen
q: they chose no longer to be under kingly government, but to have chief magistrates annually chosen, so as to be under one another’s authority by turn.

s: Pyrgo was wife of Alcathous (before he married Euæchma)
q: there are two tombs, one they say of Pyrgo, the wife of Alcathous before he married Euæchma the daughter of Megareus,

s: Apollo assisted in building Alcathous (the wall at Megara)
q: And Apollo, as the Megarians say, assisted him in building the wall, and laid his harp down on the stone:

s: Polyidus purged Alcathous (for the murder of Callipolis)
q: who went to Megara, and purged Alcathous for the murder of his son Callipolis.

s: Dionysus has near Satyr (the work of Praxiteles in Parian marble)
q: And a Satyr is near Dionysus, the work of Praxiteles in Parian marble.

s: Satyr is made by Praxiteles (in Parian marble)
q: And a Satyr is near Dionysus, the work of Praxiteles in Parian marble.

s: Aphrodite has statue a statue of the goddess (in ivory, under the title Praxis (Action))
q: and a statue of the goddess in ivory, under the title Praxis (_Action_). This is the oldest statue in the shrine. And _Persuasion_ and another goddess whom they call _Consolation_ are by Praxiteles:

s: Chance has temple by Praxiteles (in the temple near Aphrodite’s shrine)
q: And near the shrine of Aphrodite is the temple of Chance: this too is by Praxiteles.

s: Lysippus made Muses (in the neighbouring temple)
q: And in the neighbouring temple Lysippus has made the Muses and a brazen Zeus.

s: Apollo has harp placed on stone (while assisting Alcathous)
q: And near this altar is a stone, on which they say Apollo put his harp down, while he assisted Alcathous in building the wall.

s: Corœbus has tomb at Megara (in the market-place)
q: And his tomb is in the market-place at Megara:

s: Pythian Priestess instructed Corœbus (to carry a tripod from Delphi and build where it fell)
q: The Pythian priestess forbade Corœbus to return to Argos, but told him to carry a tripod from the temple, and wherever the tripod should fall, there he was to build a temple to Apollo and himself dwell.

s: Orsippus won Olympia (the foot-race prize while running naked)
q: Orsippus, who, though the athletes according to olden custom had girdles round their loins, ran naked at Olympia in the race and won the prize.

s: Alcathous sacrificed to Prodromi (when commencing to build his wall)
q: and they say that Alcathous first sacrificed to them when he was commencing to build his wall.

s: shell-like stone is used in Megara (white, softer than other stone, and containing seashells)
q: the Megarians are the only Greeks who possess this peculiar kind of stone, and many things in their city are made of it.

s: Scironian road was widened by Emperor Adrian (wide enough for two chariots abreast)
q: And the Emperor Adrian made it so wide and convenient that two chariots could drive abreast.

s: Melicerta was carried to Isthmus (by a dolphin)
q: And the boy, being carried it is said by a dolphin to the Isthmus of Corinth, had various honours paid to him under the name of Palæmon,

s: Isthmian games was celebrated for him
q: and the Isthmian games were celebrated in his honour.

s: Sciron was killed by Theseus (by being thrown into the sea)
q: for he himself was thrown by Theseus into the same sea.

s: temple of Zeus the Remover is dedicated to Zeus
q: And on the top of the mountain is a temple to Zeus called the Remover.

s: Corinth is inhabited by colonists (sent there by the Romans)
q: Now Corinth is inhabited by none of the ancient Corinthians, but by colonists who were sent there by the Romans.

s: Corinth contains Well of Glauce
q: As you go from the market-place towards Sicyon, there is visible on the right of the road a temple and brazen statue of Apollo, and at a little distance a well called the well of Glauce

s: Corinth contains Odeum of Corinth
q: Above this well is what is called the Odeum.

s: Corinth was rebuilt by Julius Cæsar
q: and they say it was rebuilt by Julius Cæsar, who instituted the present form of government at Rome, (the Imperial).

s: Romans destroyed Corinth (under Mummius the General of the Roman army)
q: but they destroyed Corinth under Mummius the General of the Roman army

s: Achaean confederacy is joined by Corinth
q: For the Corinthians joined it, and took their part in the war with the Romans

s: Poseidon is awarded Isthmus (by Briareus as arbitrator)
q: The Corinthians say that Poseidon had a controversy with the Sun about their land, and that Briareus was the Arbitrator, awarding the Isthmus and all in that direction to Poseidon

s: Poseidon has statues some Tritons (in brass)
q: And at the temple, which is not very large, there stand some Tritons in brass.

s: Poseidon has son Palemon
q: and their son Palæmon is seated bolt upright on the dolphin’s back

s: Poseidon has consort Amphitrite
q: And Amphitrite and Poseidon are standing in a chariot

s: Isthmian games are established for Melicerta (in his honour)
q: Sisyphus, finding him lying dead on the shore, buried him at the Isthmus, and established the Isthmian games in honour of him.

s: Corinth is inhabited by Romans (as colonists)
q: Now Corinth is inhabited by none of the ancient Corinthians, but by colonists who were sent there by the Romans.

s: Isthmian games continue after destruction of Corinth by Mummius (at Sicyon while Corinth was desolate)
q: And the Isthmian games did not fall into disuse when Corinth was taken by Mummius, but as long as the city lay desolate, these games took place at Sicyon

s: Isthmian games return to Corinth (after the city was rebuilt)
q: and when the city was rebuilt the old honour came back to Corinth.

s: Isthmus makes Peloponnese (a peninsula)
q: This Isthmus makes the Peloponnese a Peninsula.

s: Isthmus connects Cenchreae (to the sea on one side)
q: The Isthmus of Corinth extends in one direction to the sea near Cenchreæ, and in the other to the sea near Lechæum.

s: Isthmus connects Lechaeum (to the sea on the other side)
q: The Isthmus of Corinth extends in one direction to the sea near Cenchreæ, and in the other to the sea near Lechæum.

s: Cenchreae is named after Cenchrias
q: The Corinthian seaports got their names from Leches and Cenchrias, who were reputed to be the sons of Poseidon by Pirene the daughter of Achelous

s: Cenchreae has shrine to Aphrodite (statue in stone)
q: And at Cenchreæ there is a shrine of Aphrodite and her statue in stone

s: Lechaeum is named after Leches
q: The Corinthian seaports got their names from Leches and Cenchrias

s: Lechaeum contains Temple of Poseidon at Corinth
q: And there is at Lechæum a temple and brazen statue of Poseidon

s: Aphrodite has temple on Acrocorinth
q: On the ascent to Acro-Corinthus there is also a temple of Aphrodite

s: Corinth joins Achaean confederacy
q: For the Corinthians joined it, and took their part in the war with the Romans which Critolaus, who had been appointed commander in chief of the Achæans, brought about

s: Aphrodite receives Acrocorinth (from the Sun according to Corinthian tradition)
q: the Sun, as the Corinthians say, let Aphrodite have it

s: Bellerophon is assisted by Athene (in various ways)
q: who they say helped Bellerophon more than any of the gods in various ways, and gave him Pegasus, after having broken it in and bridled it herself.

s: Bellerophon receives Pegasus (from Athene)
q: and gave him Pegasus, after having broken it in and bridled it herself.

s: Bellerophon has temple at Corinth
q: Here is a temple of Bellerophon

s: Artemis causes death of Cenchrias (according to the story of Pirene’s transformation)
q: They say that Pirene became a well from a woman through the tears she shed, bewailing the death of her son Cenchrias at the hands of Artemis.

s: Artemis has temple at Cenchreae
q: and as you go to Cenchreæ from the Isthmus a temple of Artemis, and old wooden statue of the goddess.

s: Apollo is honoured by Tenea (as the highest honoured god)
q: and accordingly Apollo is the god they hold in highest honour.

s: Apollo has statue at Corinth (called the Clarian)
q: And there is a brazen statue of Apollo called the Clarian

s: Athene helps Bellerophon (more than any of the gods in various ways)
q: who they say helped Bellerophon more than any of the gods in various ways

s: Athene gives Pegasus (after breaking in and bridling him)
q: and gave him Pegasus, after having broken it in and bridled it herself.

s: Corinth is destroyed by destruction of Corinth by Mummius
q: but they destroyed Corinth under Mummius the General of the Roman army

s: Athene has statue at Corinth (in brass, in the middle of the market-place)
q: And in the middle of the market-place is a statue of Athene in brass

s: Medea rules Corinth (after being summoned from Iolcus)
q: when in after days Corinthus the son of Marathon died childless, the Corinthians sent for Medea from Iolcus to hand over the kingdom to her

s: Medea hands over kingdom to Sisyphus (after leaving Corinth)
q: Eventually Medea herself went away too, and handed over the kingdom to Sisyphus.

s: Acrocorinth is a hill above Corinth (the summit of the hill)
q: As you ascend to Acro-Corinthus, (it is the top of the hill above the city

s: Acrocorinth is awarded to Sun (by Briareus after litigation with Poseidon)
q: Briareus gave it to the Sun, after litigation

s: Acrocorinth contains Temple of Aphrodite on Acrocorinth
q: On the ascent to Acro-Corinthus there is also a temple of Aphrodite

s: destruction of Corinth by Mummius is carried out by Mummius (as general of the Roman army)
q: but they destroyed Corinth under Mummius the General of the Roman army

s: rebuilding of Corinth by Julius Caesar is carried out by Julius Caesar
q: and they say it was rebuilt by Julius Cæsar

s: Corinth is rebuilt by rebuilding of Corinth by Julius Caesar
q: and they say it was rebuilt by Julius Cæsar, who instituted the present form of government at Rome, (the Imperial).

s: Corinth has isthmus Isthmus
q: The Isthmus of Corinth extends in one direction to the sea near Cenchreæ, and in the other to the sea near Lechæum.

s: Corinth contains Theatre of Corinth (notable sight)
q: The great sights at Corinth are the Theatre, and the Stadium of white stone.

s: Corinth contains Stadium of Corinth (built of white stone)
q: The great sights at Corinth are the Theatre, and the Stadium of white stone.

s: Corinth has temple the temple (not very large)
q: And at the temple, which is not very large, there stand some Tritons in brass.

s: temple is located near the city (not far from)
q: there is a temple, which was burnt down, not far from the city on the left hand of the way.

s: Sicyon is near Corinth (near neighbours)
q: And the people of Sicyon, who are near neighbours to the Corinthians

s: Ægialeus is a Autochthon
q: Ægialeus the Autochthon first dwelt there

s: Ægialus is named after Ægialeus (as its king)
q: what is now called Ægialus in the Peloponnese was called after him its king

s: Ægialus is part of Peloponnese
q: what is now called Ægialus in the Peloponnese was called after him its king

s: Ægialeus founds Ægialea (a city in the plain)
q: and that he was founder of Ægialea a city in the plain

s: Ægialeus is the father of Europs
q: And they say that the son of Ægialeus was Europs

s: temple is located on coast (on the route from Corinth toward Sicyon)
q: And as you go from Corinth along the coast in the direction of Sicyon there is a temple, which was burnt down, not far from the city on the left hand of the way.

s: Poseidon is the father of Peratus (according to the account of Chalcinia’s child)
q: who they say bore a child to Poseidon, who was called Peratus

s: temple has state burnt down
q: there is a temple, which was burnt down, not far from the city on the left hand of the way.

s: Demeter rears Orthopolis (after taking compassion on Plemnæus)
q: till Demeter took compassion on him, and coming to Ægialea as a stranger to Plemnæus reared his child Orthopolis.

s: burning of the temple is caused by Pyrrhus (according to one account)
q: this was they say a temple of Apollo, and burnt down by Pyrrhus the son of Achilles.

s: temple is dedicated to Apollo (according to one account)
q: this was they say a temple of Apollo, and burnt down by Pyrrhus the son of Achilles.

s: Corinthians erect temple (to Olympian Zeus, according to another account)
q: I have also heard another account, that the Corinthians erected this temple to Olympian Zeus

s: temple is dedicated to Olympian Zeus (according to another account)
q: I have also heard another account, that the Corinthians erected this temple to Olympian Zeus

s: Epopeus is a king (of Ægialea)
q: And Corax dying childless, about this time Epopeus came from Thessaly and obtained the kingdom.

s: Thebes is bounded by the river (between Thebes and Platæa)
q: the river that forms the boundary between Thebes and Platæa

s: Thebes is ruled by Lycus (as regent for Labdacus)
q: he gave orders that Lycus his brother should be ruler of the Thebans for the present: for Nycteus himself was Regent for Labdacus

s: Zeus is father of Zethus (according to Asius)
q: Antiope, the daughter of the deep-eddying river Asopus, bare Zethus and divine Amphion, being pregnant both by Zeus, and Epopeus shepherd of his people.

s: Zeus is father of Amphion (according to Asius)
q: Antiope, the daughter of the deep-eddying river Asopus, bare Zethus and divine Amphion, being pregnant both by Zeus, and Epopeus shepherd of his people.

s: Sicyon is a king (whose name was given to the region and town)
q: and when he became king the region got called after him Sicyonia, and the town Sicyon instead of Ægialea.

s: Sicyon is son of Metion (according to the Sicyonians)
q: And the Sicyonians say that Sicyon was not the son of Marathon the son of Epopeus, but the son of Metion the son of Erechtheus.

s: Sicyonia is named after Sicyon (when Sicyon became king)
q: and when he became king the region got called after him Sicyonia, and the town Sicyon instead of Ægialea.

s: Sicyon (city) is razed by Demetrius (who built the present city on the citadel)
q: And their city, built by Ægialeus in the plain, Demetrius the son of Antigonus razed to the ground, and built the present city on the site of what was in former times the citadel.

s: Sicyon (city) is located on citadel (the site of the present city)
q: Demetrius the son of Antigonus razed to the ground, and built the present city on the site of what was in former times the citadel.

s: Dionysus has temple Temple of Dionysus at Sicyon (next to the theatre)
q: And next to the theatre is a temple of Dionysus: the god is fashioned in gold and ivory

s: Epopeus comes from Thessaly
q: And Corax dying childless, about this time Epopeus came from Thessaly and obtained the kingdom.

s: Dionysus has sacred women Bacchantes (in white stone and full of Bacchic fury)
q: and near him some Bacchantes in white stone. These women they say are sacred to Dionysus, and full of Bacchic fury.

s: Adrastus rules Sicyon (after Polybus’ death)
q: and when Adrastus fled from Argos he went to Polybus at Sicyon, and after Polybus’ death he obtained the chief power at Sicyon.

s: Adrastus is king of Argos (after his restoration)
q: But when Adrastus was restored to Argos

s: Hercules is worshipped as hero (in the older Sicyonian rite)
q: that Phæstus, when he went to Sicyon, found that the people there offered victims to Hercules as a hero

s: Hercules is worshipped as god (according to Phæstus’s view and the later rite)
q: whereas he thought they ought to sacrifice to him as to a god. And now the Sicyonians sacrifice lambs and burn their thighs on the altar

s: Apollo has temple Temple of Apollo at Sicyon (in the middle of the present market-place)
q: And that temple is in the middle of the present market-place

s: Apollo is called Lycian Apollo (Wolf-god)
q: And next is the temple of Lycian (_Wolf-god_) Apollo, in a very dilapidated condition.

s: Dorians include Sicyonians (after the Sicyonians became Dorians)
q: And the Sicyonians became Dorians after this, and a part of Argolis.

s: Argolis includes Sicyonia (after the Sicyonians became Dorians)
q: And the Sicyonians became Dorians after this, and a part of Argolis.

s: Corinth is connected by road to Sicyon (city) (the road runs from Corinth towards Sicyon)
q: And as you go from Corinth towards Sicyon you come to the tomb of Messenian Lycus

s: Epopeus builds temple to Athene (after his victory)
q: And Epopeus at first offered sacrifices for his victory and built a temple to Athene

s: Sellasia was attacked by Antigonus (in concert with the Achæans)
q: Antigonus crossed into the Peloponnese, and in concert with the Achæans attacked Cleomenes at Sellasia. And the Achæans were victorious, and Sellasia was enslaved

s: Sellasia is site of Battle of Sellasia (between Cleomenes and Antigonus with the Achæans)
q: Antigonus crossed into the Peloponnese, and in concert with the Achæans attacked Cleomenes at Sellasia.

s: Aratus is son of Clinias
q: and put in their place Clinias the father of Aratus

s: Aratus liberates Sicyon (city) (by overthrowing Nicocles)
q: And he took it by storm with no great difficulty, and Nicocles slipt out at a back door and fled. And Aratus granted the Sicyonians isonomy

s: Aratus joins Achæan league (he forced the Sicyonians into it)
q: he forced the Sicyonians, though they were Dorians, into the Achæan league.

s: Aratus is buried in Arateum (at Sicyon)
q: And from Ægium, for here fate took him, they took his body to Sicyon and buried him, and the hero-chapel Arateum is still called after him.

s: Achæan league includes Sicyonians (after Aratus compelled their entry)
q: he forced the Sicyonians, though they were Dorians, into the Achæan league.

s: Achæan league is led by Aratus (as commander in chief)
q: And forthwith he was chosen commander in chief by the Achæans

s: Macedonians has in hands the Piræus and Munychia, and moreover Salamis and Sunium
q: thought it monstrous that the Piræus and Munychia, and moreover Salamis and Sunium, should be allowed to continue in Macedonian hands

s: Philip poisons Aratus (when Aratus did not praise his temper)
q: But when Philip took the government into his own hands, because Aratus did not praise his frequent exhibition of temper to his subjects, and sometimes even checked him in his outbursts, he murdered him, giving him poison when he didn’t expect it.

s: Epopeus dies of wound (originally neglected)
q: But afterwards Epopeus chanced to die of his wound which had been originally neglected

s: Philip is father of Demetrius (whose death caused Philip’s death by sorrow)
q: for his son Demetrius was poisoned by Perseus, his youngest brother, and so caused his father’s death by sorrow.

s: Sparta is ruled by Cleomenes (as king)
q: Cleomenes, the son of Leonidas, and grandson of Cleonymus, when he succeeded to the kingdom in Sparta

s: Cleomenes is king of Sparta (before his defeat at Sellasia)
q: when he succeeded to the kingdom in Sparta

s: Cleomenes abolishes Senate (replacing its power with the Great Council of Patronomi)
q: and having put down the power of the Senate, he established instead of them The Great Council of Patronomi

s: Cleomenes is defeated at Sellasia (by Antigonus and the Achæans)
q: Antigonus crossed into the Peloponnese, and in concert with the Achæans attacked Cleomenes at Sellasia. And the Achæans were victorious

s: Lacedæmonians recover old Polity (after Antigonus and the Achæans captured Sparta)
q: Antigonus and the Achæans then gave back to the Lacedæmonians their old Polity

s: Lacedæmonians adopt republican form of government (after Cleomenes’s reign)
q: And the Lacedæmonians, glad to get rid of Cleomenes, chose to submit to kingly government no longer, but from thenceforth until now had the republican form of government.

s: Æsculapius has temple the temple of Æsculapius
q: A road leads from here to the temple of Æsculapius.

s: Æsculapius is represented as beardless (in gold and ivory by Calamis)
q: At the entrance is the god himself (Æsculapius) beardless, in gold and ivory, the work of Calamis

s: Aphrodite has temple Temple of Aphrodite at Sicyon (with restricted access)
q: Next is the temple of Aphrodite. None may enter into it but a maiden Sacristan

s: Antiope is a daughter (of Nycteus)
q: Antiope the daughter of Nycteus had a great reputation for beauty among the Greeks

s: Aphrodite is statue by Canachus (seated, in gold and ivory)
q: Her figure seated is the design of Canachus a native of Sicyon

s: Aphrodite holds poppy (in one hand)
q: The goddess wears on her head a cap, and in one hand holds a poppy, in the other an apple.

s: Aphrodite holds apple (in one hand)
q: The goddess wears on her head a cap, and in one hand holds a poppy, in the other an apple.

s: Sicyonians sacrifice to Aphrodite (burning the thighs of victims except wild boars)
q: And they offer in sacrifice to her the thighs of any victims but wild boars, all other parts they burn with juniper wood

s: Sicyonian royal succession includes Epopeus (followed by Lamedon)
q: for Lamedon (the son of Coronus) the king after Epopeus gave Antiope up.

s: Sicyonian royal succession includes Ianiscus (became king)
q: But when Adrastus was restored to Argos, then Ianiscus the descendant of Clytius, the father in law of Lamedon, came from Attica and became king

s: Sicyonian earthquake destroys Sicyon (city) (leaving it almost bare of men and destroying works of art)
q: And when they were in a far from favourable condition an earthquake came on them, and made the city almost bare of men, and robbed them of many works of art.

s: Aratus's liberation of Sicyon restores isonomy (to the Sicyonians after Nicocles fled)
q: And Aratus granted the Sicyonians isonomy, reconciling them to the refugees

s: Aratus's liberation of Sicyon restores houses and goods (to the refugees with compensation to purchasers)
q: and giving back to the refugees all their houses and goods that had been sold, but not without full compensation to former purchasers.

s: Cleomenes' war with the Achæans begins at Dyme (with Cleomenes attacking the Achæans)
q: And he attacked them and beat them at Dyme above Patræ, Aratus being in this action the Achæan general

s: Antiope is reputed daughter of Asopus (according to a rumour)
q: and there was a rumour about her that she was the daughter of Asopus, the river that forms the boundary between Thebes and Platæa, and not the daughter of Nycteus.

s: Cleomenes' war with the Achæans compels Aratus (to invite Antigonus’s aid)
q: and this defeat it was that compelled Aratus to invite the aid of Antigonus

s: Battle of Sellasia is won by the Achæans
q: Antigonus crossed into the Peloponnese, and in concert with the Achæans attacked Cleomenes at Sellasia. And the Achæans were victorious

s: poisoning of Aratus is committed by Philip (unexpectedly)
q: he murdered him, giving him poison when he didn’t expect it.

s: Antiope is taken to Thebes (after Lamedon gave her up)
q: so Lycus had no longer any need of war, for Lamedon (the son of Coronus) the king after Epopeus gave Antiope up. And she, as she was being conducted to Thebes

s: Antiope gives birth to a child (near Eleutheræ)
q: And she, as she was being conducted to Thebes, gave birth to a child on the road near Eleutheræ.

s: Antiope is statue in precincts sacred to Aphrodite
q: And there are other precincts there sacred to Aphrodite: and in them first is the statue of Antiope.

s: Epopeus builds temple to Artemis and Apollo (neighbouring)
q: And they say that Epopeus built the neighbouring temple to Artemis and Apollo,

s: Adrastus builds temple next to Hera
q: and Adrastus the one next to Hera:

s: Adrastus builds altar to Pan (behind the temple of Hera)
q: Adrastus also built behind the temple of Hera two altars, one to Pan, and one to the Sun God in white stone.

s: Adrastus builds altar to the Sun God (behind the temple of Hera; in white stone)
q: Adrastus also built behind the temple of Hera two altars, one to Pan, and one to the Sun God in white stone.

s: Demeter rears son of Plemnæus
q: Plemnæus built it in gratitude to the goddess for rearing his son.

q: and there are statues of Dionysus and Demeter and Proserpine (showing only their faces) in the

q: and there are statues of Dionysus and Demeter and Proserpine (showing only their faces) in the

q: and there are statues of Dionysus and Demeter and Proserpine (showing only their faces) in the

s: Sicyon is connected by road to Phlius (straight road; about ten stades)
q: And as you go from Sicyon on the straight road to Phlius, about ten stades,

s: Epopeus erects shrine of Athene (formerly)
q: which Epopeus formerly erected, in size and beauty surpassing those of its time.

s: Titan is a brother of the Sun
q: where the natives say Titan first dwelt, who was the brother of the Sun,

s: Titan first dwells at Titane
q: where the natives say Titan first dwelt, who was the brother of the Sun, and gave the name Titane to this place.

s: Titan gives name to Titane
q: and gave the name Titane to this place.

s: Titan is associated with Sun (because he watched the seasons and the Sun fructified and ripened seeds and fruit)
q: This Titan seems to me to have been wonderfully clever in watching the seasons of the year, as when the Sun fructified and ripened seeds and fruit, and this was why he was considered the Sun’s brother.

s: Alexanor is a son of Machaon
q: And afterwards Alexanor, the son of Machaon, the son of Æsculapius, came to Sicyon,

s: Machaon is a son of Æsculapius
q: Alexanor, the son of Machaon, the son of Æsculapius,

s: Alexanor builds temple of Æsculapius at Titane (at Titane)
q: came to Sicyon, and built a temple of Æsculapius at Titane.

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane is in Titane
q: built a temple of Æsculapius at Titane.

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane has residents suppliants of Æsculapius (for the most part)
q: A few people dwell there, but for the most part only the suppliants of the god,

s: Æsculapius has statue statue of Æsculapius (only the face, fingers, and toes are visible; covered by a white woollen tunic and cloak)
q: The only parts of the statue that are visible are the face and fingers and toes, for a white woollen tunic and cloak are thrown round it.

s: Alexanor may have made statue of Æsculapius (some say)
q: nor do they know who made it, though some say Alexanor himself.

s: Hygiea has statue statue of Hygiea (somewhat similar to the statue of Æsculapius)
q: And there is a statue of Hygiea somewhat similar.

s: Hygiea receives women's shorn hair (as an offering)
q: the hair of the women which they shear to the goddess,

s: Hygiea has statue clothed in Babylonish garment (in folds)
q: and by the folds of a Babylonish garment.

s: Hygiea is worshipped by those seeking propitiation (whichever deity they wish to propitiate)
q: And whichever of these any one wishes to propitiate, he is instructed to worship Hygiea.

s: Alexanor receives sacrifices sacrifices (after sunset, as to a hero)
q: to the former they offer sacrifices after sunset as to a hero,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Hercules (figure on the gable ends)
q: On the gable ends are figures of Hercules, and several Victories.

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Victories (figures on the gable ends)
q: On the gable ends are figures of Hercules, and several Victories.

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Dionysus (wooden statue in the porch)
q: And in the porch are statues of Dionysus and Hecate and Aphrodite and The Mother of the Gods and Fortune: these are all in wood,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Hecate (wooden statue in the porch)
q: And in the porch are statues of Dionysus and Hecate and Aphrodite and The Mother of the Gods and Fortune: these are all in wood,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Aphrodite (wooden statue in the porch)
q: And in the porch are statues of Dionysus and Hecate and Aphrodite and The Mother of the Gods and Fortune: these are all in wood,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Mother of the Gods (wooden statue in the porch)
q: And in the porch are statues of Dionysus and Hecate and Aphrodite and The Mother of the Gods and Fortune: these are all in wood,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Fortune (wooden statue in the porch)
q: And in the porch are statues of Dionysus and Hecate and Aphrodite and The Mother of the Gods and Fortune: these are all in wood,

s: temple of Æsculapius at Titane contains Gortynian Æsculapius (stone statue in the porch)
q: and one of Gortynian Æsculapius in stone.

s: Granianus competes in pentathlum (at Olympia)
q: He won two victories at Olympia in the pentathlum,

s: Titane contains temple of Athene
q: And at Titane there is also a temple of Athene, into which they carry the statue of Coronis.

s: Phliasia has chief town Phlius
q: Next to Sicyonia is Phliasia. Its chief town Phlius is 40 stades at most distant from Titane

s: Phlius is a city (chief town of Phliasia)
q: Its chief town Phlius is 40 stades at most distant from Titane

s: Phliasians are not connected with Arcadians (according to the catalogue in Homer’s Iliad)
q: That the Phliasians have no connection with the Arcadians is plain from the catalogue of the Arcadians in Homer’s Iliad, for they are not included among them.

s: Phliasians are originally Argives (according to their tradition)
q: And that they were Argives originally, and became Dorians after the return of the Heraclidæ to the Peloponnese

s: Phliasians become Dorians (after the return of the Heraclidæ)
q: became Dorians after the return of the Heraclidæ to the Peloponnese

s: Heraclidæ return to Peloponnese
q: after the return of the Heraclidæ to the Peloponnese

s: Aras is a Autochthon (first person said to have lived in Phliasian land)
q: The first person who lived in this land was they say Aras an Autochthon

s: Aras builds Arantia (on the Arantine hill)
q: Here he built his city, and from him both land and city got called of old Arantia.

s: Athene has statue old wooden statue of Athene (at Titane)
q: And in it is an old wooden statue of Athene.

s: Aras has son Aoris
q: And Aras had a son Aoris and a daughter Aræthyrea

s: Aras has daughter Aræthyrea
q: And Aras had a son Aoris and a daughter Aræthyrea

s: Phlias is a son of Dionysus (according to the Phliasian tradition)
q: for I know that he was called the son of Dionysus, and was said to have been one of those who sailed in the Argo.

s: Phlias sails in Argo
q: was said to have been one of those who sailed in the Argo.

s: Phlias is child of Aræthyrea (mother)
q: And Aræthyrea was the mother of Phlias and not Chthonophyle

s: Phlias is married to Chthonophyle
q: for Chthonophyle was his wife and he had Andromedas by her.

s: Phlius is attacked by Rhegnidas (a Dorian)
q: Rhegnidas a Dorian (the son of Phalces the son of Temenus) marched against it from Argos and Sicyon.

s: Rhegnidas is a Dorian (son of Phalces)
q: Rhegnidas a Dorian (the son of Phalces the son of Temenus)

s: Hippasus opposes Rhegnidas (advocating vigorous defence)
q: But Hippasus and his party stood out for a vigorous defence

s: Hippasus flees to Samos (with his supporters)
q: Hippasus and those who agreed with him fled to Samos.

s: Pythagoras is descendant of Hippasus (great-grandson)
q: And the great grandson of this Hippasus was Pythagoras, surnamed the Wise

s: Hebe is a goddess (called Ganymeda by the most ancient Phliasians)
q: The deity to whom the temple belongs is said by the most ancient of the Phliasians to have been Ganymeda, but by later ones Hebe

s: Hebe is wife of Hercules (according to Homer)
q: he has said that she was the wife of Hercules.

s: Celeæ is a place (about five stades from Phlius)
q: Now Celeæ is about five stades from Phlius

s: Celeæ sacrifices to Demeter (every fourth year and not annually)
q: and they sacrifice to Demeter there every fourth year and not annually.

s: Dysaules establishes mysteries of Demeter (at Celeæ according to Phliasian tradition)
q: this Dysaules established the mysteries here

s: Dysaules is buried at Celeæ
q: There is also here as I have said the tomb of Dysaules

s: Cleonæ is a town (small town on the road from Corinth to Argos)
q: On the road from Corinth to Argos you come to the small town of Cleonæ.

s: Nemea has temple Nemean Zeus (the roof has fallen in and the statue is gone)
q: At Nemea is a temple well worth seeing of Nemean Zeus, only the roof has tumbled in, and there is no longer any statue there

s: Nemea contains tomb of Opheltes (enclosed by a stone wall with altars)
q: Here too is the tomb of Opheltes, and round it a wall of stones, and altars within the precincts
